title: The mayor and Montaigne
hookLine: elected mayor of Bordeaux, he says the mayor and Montaigne were always two (Essays 3.10)

cards: The man who walked away from public life to sit in a tower with his books gets called back. The city of Bordeaux elects him mayor, and Montaigne takes the job.

Then, in an essay of book three about managing your own will, he says something like a riddle: the mayor and Montaigne have always been two, clearly separated. Same body, same signature, same house. Two.
What could that mean, and why would anyone want it?

teach.h: PLAY THE PART AS A PART.
teach.b: First, the part in a play. We should play our part well, Montaigne says, but as a part, a borrowed character. The mask is real and the work is real, but the mask isn't the face.
He warns against people who let the office soak into them, who become their title all the way down and carry it home to the dinner table. Second, how deep the job goes.

teach.h: IN THE HANDS, NOT THE LIVER.
teach.b: He'll take the city's affairs into his hands, he says, but not into his lungs and liver. He'll carry the work; he won't let it eat him. That isn't laziness; it keeps him clear enough to do the work well.
Third, the critics. Some said his time as mayor left little mark, that he was too easygoing. He doesn't hide it.
He answers that he kept things calm, did no harm, and didn't stir up trouble just to look busy.
Readers can judge whether that's enough, but he's honest about the trade he chose. Fourth, why two matters.
When the role and the person are fused, every attack on the work feels like an attack on the self, and losing the job feels like losing who you are.

teach.h: GIVE YOUR BEST, GO HOME AS YOU.
teach.b: When they're two, you can give the role your best and still go home as yourself.
Manager, nurse, parent on duty, the one who always fixes things: do it fully, then take off the badge.

how: Readers of Montaigne often quote his line that the mayor and Montaigne were always two as a picture of doing a public role fully while keeping the self distinct from it.

games.q: what does “the mayor and montaigne” mean?
o: a feud between Montaigne and the mayor of his city
a role worn fully, with a self kept apart underneath
a city law that let one man hold two offices

games.q: the mayor and Montaigne: tap the pairs.
p: in his hands, not his liver

s: Montaigne refused to serve as mayor of Bordeaux
he took the office, and wrote about keeping himself distinct from it.
he says the mayor and Montaigne were always two
same man, but the role and the self clearly separated.
he hides the criticism of his time in office
he admits some said he left little mark, and answers that he kept things calm.

games.q: you're Montaigne, and the city has made you mayor. how do you hold the job?
o: let the office become your whole life.
serve fully, but keep the mayor and yourself as two.
accept the title and do nothing.
games.why: he plays the part well, as a part. the city's affairs go into his hands, not into his lungs and liver.

practice: Name one role you carry, at work, at home or in your town, and picture it as a coat: how it sits on your shoulders, what it asks of you, what you're proud of in it.
Now imagine hanging it on a hook by the door; it will be there when you need it. Underneath is just you, breathing.

wordCard.voice: The mayor and Montaigne. A role worn fully, and a self kept distinct underneath it. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: two, not one. The coat waits by the door, and you walk in as yourself. Rest well.

sources.ref: Montaigne, Essays 3.10, Of husbanding your will (the mayor and Montaigne always two; playing our part as a borrowed character; affairs in the hands, not in the lungs and liver; critics of his time as mayor)
